items.article_text_original: Vaccination gaps and increased population movement could facilitate further transmission, underscoring the need for stronger vaccination and surveillance efforts Washington, D.C., 9 October 2026 (PAHO) — With several religious mass gatherings in South America expected to increase national and international travel across the Americas in the coming months, the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) is urging countries to strengthen vaccination, surveillance and rapid response measures as the risk of measles spread across the Region remains very high. The warning comes in a new PAHO regional risk assessment released amid ongoing outbreaks, persistent gaps in vaccination coverage and the detection of measles cases in new geographic areas. The assessment updates PAHO’s regional evaluation of 5 August 2026, with a specific focus on risks associated with upcoming religious mass gatherings in South America and their potential implications for the Region of the Americas. “Measles is highly contagious, and we are seeing the consequences of gaps in vaccination coverage across the Americas,” said Dr. Jarbas Barbosa, PAHO Director. “People need to protect their children with the very effective and safe measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine, and countries have to close immunity gaps, strengthen surveillance and ensure that they can detect and respond rapidly to cases, particularly as increased travel and large gatherings create more opportunities for the virus to spread.” According to the latest PAHO data, 55,792 confirmed measles cases and 77 deaths were reported in 17 countries and territories in the Region between 4 January and 3 October 2026. This represents a 4.8-fold increase in cases compared with the same period in 2025. Measles cases have also increased globally in 2026, increasing the likelihood of imported cases through international travel and onward transmission in communities with low immunity. Guatemala reported the largest number of cases, followed by Mexico, the United States, Peru and Canada. Together, these five countries accounted for 99.5% of confirmed cases in the Region. Cases have also been reported in Argentina, Belize, Bolivia, Bonaire, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, El Salvador, Honduras, Panama and Uruguay. Why mass gatherings increase the risk Measles is highly contagious and can spread rapidly when introduced into populations with low immunity, particularly in crowded settings. People with measles can transmit the virus before the characteristic rash appears, meaning infected travelers may unknowingly expose others. Large gatherings and the movement of people between countries and communities can therefore facilitate the importation and onward spread of the virus. “Anyone planning to attend a large gathering should check that they are protected against measles,” said Dr. Daniel Salas, Executive Manager of Comprehensive Immunization at PAHO. “Even people travelling within their own country may be exposed when large numbers of people from different regions come together. People aged 6 months and older who do not have evidence of vaccination should receive a dose of measles-rubella vaccine before traveling or attending the gathering, preferably at least two weeks in advance.” Vaccination remains the main protection Regional coverage reached 88% for the first dose of the MMR vaccine and 85% for the second dose in 2025, below the 95% coverage needed to prevent outbreaks. Persistent low coverage has increased the number of people susceptible to measles and created pockets of susceptible populations in parts of the Region. These gaps reflect several factors, including setbacks in immunization accumulated during the COVID-19 pandemic, vaccine hesitancy in some communities, operational challenges in delivering vaccination and barriers to accessing health services, particularly among Indigenous peoples, migrants and displaced populations. An estimated 1.6 million children in the Region of the Americas did not receive any dose of measles vaccine in 2025. PAHO supports countries to strengthen preparedness PAHO is working with countries across the Region to strengthen vaccination, surveillance and outbreak response. In South America, the Organization is supporting preparedness for upcoming mass gatherings expected to involve significant national and international population movement. PAHO is also supporting laboratory-based surveillance and genomic monitoring across the Region, while affected countries are receiving technical cooperation to strengthen vaccination, contact tracing and outbreak response. PAHO urges countries to close vaccination gaps Measles can cause serious illness and complications at any age, with infants and adults at greater risk of severe disease and death. Children under five and populations experiencing malnutrition or limited access to health services have been disproportionately affected during recent outbreaks in the Region. With active outbreaks continuing and major gatherings approaching, PAHO is urging countries to use every opportunity to ensure that people who are not protected against measles have access to vaccination, while strengthening surveillance and maintaining the capacity to detect and respond rapidly to cases.

items.article_text_original: Pneumococcal Vaccine Factsheet – Information for Patients, Parents and Carers Patient factsheet providing information on pneumococcal disease and pneumococcal vaccination. Documents Details Pneumococcal disease can affect people of any age, but serious illness is more common in young children, older adults and people with certain medical conditions or weakened immune systems. Vaccination is one of the safest and most effective ways to protect people who are at increased risk of serious pneumococcal disease. Pneumococcal vaccines have been used in the UK for decades and have been rigorously assessed for safety, quality and effectiveness. Their safety continues to be monitored through the Yellow Card scheme. This factsheet is designed to help patients, parents and carers understand pneumococcal vaccines authorised and used in the UK. It covers: - Overview of pneumococcal disease - Pneumococcal vaccination and eligibility - Types of pneumococcal vaccine available in the UK - Getting the pneumococcal vaccine at the same time as other vaccinations - Safety and effectiveness of pneumococcal vaccines - Pneumococcal vaccine side effects - Pneumococcal vaccination and pregnancy - Who should not receive the pneumococcal vaccine - Report side effects to the Yellow Card scheme

items.article_text_original: At the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, we rely on our many advisory committees to help us make sound decisions based on the best science available. The FDA’s complex and multifaceted mission includes evaluating new medical devices and medicines, including vaccines and other therapies, to determine if they are safe and effective for their intended use. FDA advisory committees give our own agency experts outside, independent, and professional advice on various complex scientific, technical, and policy issues. Good scientific deliberation benefits from a range of qualified voices and perspectives. Advisory committees work because they bring perspectives that are independent of the FDA, from the research bench, the clinic, and the community. Advisory committee meetings can include a broad scientific discussion about important topics. They can also be more focused on a specific product under FDA review. Expertise, Transparency, and an Outside Viewpoint The FDA has about 50 technical and scientific advisory committees and panels, which include scientific experts and members of the public. Members are selected by their expertise to meet the needs of each specific committee’s function and topic area. Science-oriented professionals – such as physician-researchers, statisticians, engineers, medical faculty, chemists, and biologists – are represented on the committees. In addition, each committee typically includes a consumer representative and an industry representative and, based on the meeting topic, a patient representative who provides the patient or caregiver experience for a particular disease, condition, or medical product. The FDA uses advisory committees to: - Get advice from experts who work outside the agency. - Work toward an open and transparent government. - Encourage patients, health care providers, and other interested people to share their views during the open public hearing or by submitting comments to the open docket. Committees Provide Scientific, Medical Advice The primary role of FDA advisory committees is to provide independent expert advice as we evaluate products, helping us make sound decisions based on the available science. The committees review and evaluate data about the safety, effectiveness, and appropriate use of products that are intended for use in the prevention, treatment, mitigation, or diagnosis of human diseases and conditions – and any other products the FDA regulates. These include issues related to human drugs, biological products, medical devices, tobacco, and toxicology. Committees also consider general policy matters and the quality and relevance of the FDA’s research program, which provides scientific support for the regulation of these products. The committees’ discussions are designed to help ensure that the public is clear about the FDA’s expectations for data to support the safety and effectiveness of products, so that the public can be confident that the required regulatory standards will be met. This process is transparent and independent, and open to the public. Members of the public have an opportunity to address the committee and share their insight. Advisory committees make nonbinding recommendations to the FDA, which generally follows the recommendations but is not legally bound to do so. The available science and data guide the agency’s decision-making. The FDA generally makes advisory committee meeting materials available to the public no later than two business days before any meeting. These materials include an agenda and background information from the FDA and other information as appropriate. These committees are a valuable resource and make important contributions to FDA’s decision-making processes. items.article_text_original: Health authorities approved new regional strategies to strengthen preparedness for health emergencies, tackle antimicrobial resistance, curb dengue and other arboviral diseases, and improve food safety, while advancing access to vaccines, medicines and other essential health technologies across the Americas. Washington, D.C., 2 October 2026 (PAHO) – The 63rd Directing Council of the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) concluded with countries of the Americas approving a series of decisions aimed at strengthening preparedness for increasingly frequent health emergencies, addressing antimicrobial resistance, reducing the growing burden of dengue and other arboviral diseases, improving food safety, and expanding access to health technologies. Over five days, Ministers of Health and other senior health authorities from across the Americas met in Washington, D.C., to discuss key public health priorities, review progress on regional initiatives and adopt decisions aimed at strengthening health systems and advancing health and well-being across the Region. “The resolutions and decisions adopted during this Council will guide our work in the years ahead. But their true value will not be measured by what was approved in this room. It will be measured by what changes in the lives of the people we serve,” said PAHO Director Dr. Jarbas Barbosa. Strengthening health security One of the key outcomes of the meeting was the approval of the Strategy for Strengthening Health Emergency and Risk Management for Health Security 2026–2031, which seeks to strengthen countries’ capacity to prevent, prepare for and respond to health emergencies, while building safer and more resilient health services and systems and enhancing regional cooperation. The strategy comes as the Americas face increasingly frequent disasters, outbreaks and other health threats. Between 2021 and 2024, nearly 30% of all disasters recorded worldwide occurred in the Region. Member States also approved the Plan of Action on Antimicrobial Resistance 2027–2031, which promotes a One Health approach and seeks to strengthen surveillance, laboratory capacity, infection prevention and control, appropriate use of antimicrobials, and access to diagnostics and vaccines. The Council also approved the Integrated Management Strategy for the Prevention and Control of Arboviral Diseases 2026–2035, strengthening regional action on diseases such as dengue, chikungunya and Zika through improved surveillance, prevention, vector control, clinical care and outbreak response. The strategy was adopted following the largest dengue epidemic on record in the Americas. In 2024, countries reported more than 13 million dengue cases and over 8,400 deaths across the Region. A new Strategy and Plan of Action on Food Safety 2026–2031 will support countries in strengthening food safety systems, surveillance, laboratory services and risk-based approaches to reduce foodborne diseases and improve coordination across sectors. The new framework addresses a significant public health challenge in the Americas, where foodborne diseases affect an estimated 43.7 million people and cause around 78,000 deaths each year. Strengthening access to health technologies Countries also advanced efforts to strengthen and modernize PAHO’s Regional Revolving Funds, which support access to vaccines, medicines, diagnostics and other essential health technologies. “These mechanisms allow countries to continue expanding access to vaccines, medicines, diagnostics and other essential health technologies that save lives every day in our Region,” Dr. Barbosa said. The changes seek to make the Funds more efficient, flexible and sustainable while maintaining pooled procurement as an important mechanism for improving access to quality-assured health products at affordable prices. Over the last biennium alone, PAHO’s Regional Revolving Funds helped protect an estimated 170 million people through pooled procurement and shared financing mechanisms. Advancing health across the Americas The 63rd Directing Council also addressed priorities including disease elimination, primary health care and digital health, while providing a platform for countries to share experiences and solutions to strengthen health systems. During the week, PAHO presented a new edition of Health in the Americas, which found that nearly 40% of the Region’s disease burden could potentially be avoided through stronger prevention, earlier diagnosis and treatment, and more effective health systems. The Council also recognized disease-elimination achievements over the past year in Brazil, Chile, El Salvador, The Bahamas and Turks and Caicos Islands, including landmark advances against HIV, leprosy, trachoma, rabies and hepatitis B, underscoring the progress that can be achieved through sustained political commitment, strong health systems, scientific evidence and regional cooperation. PAHO also marked the 50th anniversary of its Emergency Program, recognizing five decades of support to countries in preparing for, responding to and recovering from some of the most complex health emergencies faced by the Region. Beyond the deliberations of the Directing Council, the week also included the 78th Session of the WHO Regional Committee for the Americas, where health authorities discussed global and regional health priorities, including the future financing of global health and WHO's work across the Region. Speaking virtually, WHO Director-General Dr. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus highlighted the Americas' progress in health emergency preparedness, disease elimination, digital health and regional cooperation, pointing to PAHO's Regional Revolving Funds as one of the world's most successful examples of solidarity in action. He noted that these achievements "reflect political leadership, the commitment of health workers and communities, and the enduring value of regional cooperation." “Throughout this week, we have seen once again that the diversity of our Region is one of our greatest strengths. No country has all the answers. But together, we possess an extraordinary wealth of experience, expertise, and creativity,” Dr. Barbosa said. “As we leave this meeting, let us keep the dialogue alive, exchanging ideas, learning from one another, and engaging in the constructive debate that strengthens our decisions and our institutions,” Dr. Barbosa said. The decisions adopted this week are expected to strengthen the Region’s ability to prevent and respond to health threats, expand access to health technologies and advance stronger, more resilient health systems across the Americas in the years ahead.

items.article_text_original: Washington, D.C., 30 September 2026 (PAHO) – Health leaders from across the Americas have adopted a new regional Plan of Action on Antimicrobial Resistance (AMR) 2027–2031, aimed at strengthening efforts to prevent, detect and respond to drug-resistant infections while protect the effectiveness of life-saving medicines. Approved during the 63rd Directing Council of the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), the plan provides a regional framework to support countries in updating and implementing national action plans on AMR and advancing coordinated action across human, animal and environmental health. Antimicrobial resistance occurs when bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites no longer respond to medicines, making infections more difficult to treat and increasing the risk of severe illness and death. In the Americas, bacterial AMR was associated with an estimated 569,000 deaths in 2019, including 141,000 deaths directly attributable to resistance. “The plan is the result of a collective and constructive effort by countries and partners across the Americas, reflecting a strong shared commitment to protecting public health and ensuring that antimicrobials remain effective,” said PAHO Director, Dr. Jarbas Barbosa. The plan establishes six strategic lines of action to accelerate the regional response to AMR: - Increase awareness and promote social and behavioral change to reduce the inappropriate use of antimicrobials; - Strengthening surveillance systems and laboratory networks to generate timely, high-quality data on antimicrobial resistance and use; - Intensifying infection prevention and control, including through improved water, sanitation and hygiene, stronger immunization programmes and measures to reduce infections in health care and community settings; - Promoting access to and appropriate use and safe disposal of antimicrobials, as well as access to effective diagnostics and vaccines; - Accelerating research and innovation to improve understanding of the burden of AMR and identify effective, sustainable interventions; and - Strengthening multisectoral governance, financing and accountability to ensure that AMR remains integrated into national health and development priorities. The plan emphasizes that prevention is central to tackling AMR. Strong infection prevention and control, access to clean water and sanitation, food safety and immunization can reduce infections and, consequently, the need for antimicrobial treatment. Appropriate prescribing and use of antimicrobials, supported by access to timely and accurate diagnostics, can also help slow the emergence and spread of resistance. Countries in the Americas have made important progress in recent years. Thirty of the 33 Member States that periodically report to PAHO have introduced national action plans on AMR, while 22 have established or expanded infection prevention and control programmes and antimicrobial stewardship initiatives. However, significant gaps remain in surveillance, laboratory capacity, access to quality-assured medicines and diagnostics, infection prevention and control, and sustainable financing. “Antimicrobial resistance knows no borders and cannot be addressed by any country or sector alone. Protecting the effectiveness of antimicrobials requires coordinated action, backed by strong surveillance, prevention and access to appropriate treatment,” added Dr. Sylvain Aldighieri, Director of the Department of Communicable Diseases Prevention, Control and Elimination at PAHO. The plan promotes a One Health approach, recognizing the interconnectedness of human, animal, and environmental health and encouraging collaboration across health, agriculture, food production, environmental and other sectors. It also calls for meaningful participation by health professionals, academia, civil society and communities. Through the Plan of Action on Antimicrobial Resistance 2027–2031, countries of the Americas are reinforcing regional cooperation to preserve the effectiveness of antimicrobials, protect patients and health workers, and safeguard the capacity of health systems to prevent and treat infections now and in the future.
